sections.heading: C — Stopping distances, night driving, roadside emergencies, crashes and deer
sections.markdown:
## C — Stopping distances, night driving, roadside emergencies, crashes and deer

FACT_ID: sec14-F01 | anchor: A01
Stopping distance depends on fatigue, attention, the vehicle's type and weight, tire and brake condition, road surface and weather. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-mi-s:michigan-department-of-state-secretary-o:handbook:pdf-0078]

FACT_ID: sec14-F02 | anchor: A01
On dry or wet pavement, a following distance of 3 to 4 seconds is required. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-mi-s:michigan-department-of-state-secretary-o:handbook:pdf-0078]

FACT_ID: sec14-F03 | anchor: A01
To check following distance, count one-thousand-one through one-thousand-three from when the vehicle ahead passes a fixed point; reaching that point before you finish counting 3 seconds means you are too close. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-mi-s:michigan-department-of-state-secretary-o:handbook:pdf-0078]

FACT_ID: sec14-F04 | anchor: A01
At higher speeds or in adverse conditions, stretch your following distance to 6 seconds or more if needed. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-mi-s:michigan-department-of-state-secretary-o:handbook:pdf-0078]

FACT_ID: sec14-F05 | anchor: A01
Wet pavement needs more stopping time and space; for a smooth stop, press the brake gradually harder and ease off just before stopping. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-mi-s:michigan-department-of-state-secretary-o:handbook:pdf-0078]

FACT_ID: sec14-F06 | anchor: A01
Look 20 to 30 seconds down the road to spot hazards early and avoid last-second reactions. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-mi-s:michigan-department-of-state-secretary-o:handbook:pdf-0078]

FACT_ID: sec14-F07 | anchor: A01
Anticipate problems, keep a safe gap, and allow even more stopping time on poor or slippery roads. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-mi-s:michigan-department-of-state-secretary-o:handbook:pdf-0078]

FACT_ID: sec14-F08 | anchor: A01
Headlights must be on from one half-hour after sunset to one half-hour before sunrise, and whenever visibility is reduced. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-mi-s:michigan-department-of-state-secretary-o:handbook:pdf-0078]

FACT_ID: sec14-F09 | anchor: A01
Use low beams in daytime fog, rain or snow, and turn headlights on whenever you are in doubt, since if you cannot see others they cannot see you. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-mi-s:michigan-department-of-state-secretary-o:handbook:pdf-0078]

FACT_ID: sec14-F10 | anchor: A01
Headlights are required whenever daylight is too dim to clearly see people and vehicles at 500 feet, and using only parking lights then is illegal. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-mi-s:michigan-department-of-state-secretary-o:handbook:pdf-0078]

FACT_ID: sec14-F11 | anchor: A01
At night, drive so you can stop within the distance your headlights show. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-mi-s:michigan-department-of-state-secretary-o:handbook:pdf-0078]

FACT_ID: sec14-F12 | anchor: A01
Using or even flashing high beams within 500 feet of an oncoming vehicle is illegal, and you should also dim them for pedestrians and cyclists. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-mi-s:michigan-department-of-state-secretary-o:handbook:pdf-0078]

FACT_ID: sec14-F13 | anchor: A01
If an oncoming driver keeps high beams on, look toward the right edge of the road rather than into the glare, which can blind you for several seconds and is worse through a dirty windshield. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-mi-s:michigan-department-of-state-secretary-o:handbook:pdf-0078]

FACT_ID: sec14-F14 | anchor: A01
Do not use high beams behind other vehicles, because the glare in their mirrors distracts them. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-mi-s:michigan-department-of-state-secretary-o:handbook:pdf-0078]

FACT_ID: sec14-F15 | anchor: A01
From 2014 to 2018, about 10 percent of pedestrian traffic deaths involved a roadside emergency. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-mi-s:michigan-department-of-state-secretary-o:handbook:pdf-0078]

FACT_ID: sec14-F16 | anchor: A01
In a roadside emergency the safest choice is generally to stay in the car with your seat belt buckled until help arrives. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-mi-s:michigan-department-of-state-secretary-o:handbook:pdf-0078]

FACT_ID: sec14-F17 | anchor: A02
Leaving the scene of a crash you are involved in is illegal and can bring fines, jail or both, with heavier penalties if alcohol, injuries or deaths are involved. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-mi-s:michigan-department-of-state-secretary-o:handbook:pdf-0079]

FACT_ID: sec14-F18 | anchor: A02
After a crash, help get medical aid for anyone injured. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-mi-s:michigan-department-of-state-secretary-o:handbook:pdf-0079]

FACT_ID: sec14-F19 | anchor: A02
If no one is seriously hurt or killed and the vehicle can be driven safely, a licensed driver or passenger must move it off the main road to a safe spot such as the shoulder, median or a nearby parking lot. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-mi-s:michigan-department-of-state-secretary-o:handbook:pdf-0079]

FACT_ID: sec14-F20 | anchor: A02
Exchange names, addresses, license numbers, registration and insurance information with the other drivers. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-mi-s:michigan-department-of-state-secretary-o:handbook:pdf-0079]

FACT_ID: sec14-F21 | anchor: A02
Notify police when a crash causes injuries or more than $1,000 in property damage. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-mi-s:michigan-department-of-state-secretary-o:handbook:pdf-0079]

FACT_ID: sec14-F22 | anchor: A02
Michigan has about 60,000 vehicle-deer crashes a year, and officials suspect up to half go unreported. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-mi-s:michigan-department-of-state-secretary-o:handbook:pdf-0079]

FACT_ID: sec14-F23 | anchor: A02
The average deer crash causes $2,100 in damage, usually to the front end, and statewide costs are estimated at $130 million a year. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-mi-s:michigan-department-of-state-secretary-o:handbook:pdf-0079]

FACT_ID: sec14-F24 | anchor: A02
Report a deer crash to local police, the county sheriff, Michigan State Police or the Department of Natural Resources, who can issue a permit to keep the deer. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-mi-s:michigan-department-of-state-secretary-o:handbook:pdf-0079]

FACT_ID: sec14-F25 | anchor: A02
To avoid deer, stay aware, awake, alert and sober, always wear a seat belt, and watch for deer crossing signs. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-mi-s:michigan-department-of-state-secretary-o:handbook:pdf-0079]

FACT_ID: sec14-F26 | anchor: A02
Be especially alert in fall and spring and at dawn and dusk, though deer crashes happen year-round. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-mi-s:michigan-department-of-state-secretary-o:handbook:pdf-0079]

FACT_ID: sec14-F27 | anchor: A02
If you see one deer, slow down, because deer usually travel in groups. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-mi-s:michigan-department-of-state-secretary-o:handbook:pdf-0079]

FACT_ID: sec14-F28 | anchor: A02
Deer whistles, flashing high beams and honking do not keep deer away. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-mi-s:michigan-department-of-state-secretary-o:handbook:pdf-0079]

FACT_ID: sec14-F29 | anchor: A02
If hitting a deer is unavoidable, do not swerve: stay in your lane, brake firmly, grip the wheel with both hands, come to a controlled stop, and steer well off the road. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-mi-s:michigan-department-of-state-secretary-o:handbook:pdf-0079]
